title: Kotak Downgrades Infosys, TCS, and LTIMindtree as IT Stocks Slide on AI and Visa Concerns
excerpt: The brokerage reverses its earlier buy ratings on India's top IT exporters, preferring mid-tier challengers as the Nifty IT index extends its 20%-plus decline in 2026.
body:
• Kotak Institutional Equities has downgraded Infosys, TCS, and LTIMindtree, reversing earlier buy ratings as it turns cautious on India's largest IT exporters amid accelerating AI disruption
  • The brokerage now prefers mid-tier "challengers" — firms like Coforge and Persistent Systems — over Tier-1 incumbents, citing faster growth and better positioning for AI-era contracts
  • IT stocks fell sharply following the downgrade, with TCS and Infosys leading losses as H-1B visa policy concerns added additional pressure
  • The Nifty IT index has declined more than 20% year-to-date, with roughly $73 billion in market value erased from India's IT sector in 2026

Kotak Institutional Equities has turned meaningfully more cautious on India's biggest IT services companies, downgrading Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, and LTIMindtree in a report that marks a significant shift from its earlier stance favoring Tier-1 incumbents. The brokerage now prefers what it calls "quality challengers" — mid-tier firms it believes are better positioned to win in an industry being reshaped by artificial intelligence.

A Major Reversal

As recently as June 2026, Kotak maintained buy ratings on TCS, Infosys, and Tech Mahindra among large-cap IT companies, while keeping reduce ratings on HCL Technologies, LTIMindtree, and Mphasis, and a sell on Wipro. The new report represents a significant downward revision in the brokerage's outlook on the very companies it previously backed.

The downgrades of Infosys and TCS are particularly notable given their status as the two largest Indian IT companies by market capitalization and revenue. Both have been staples in most domestic brokerage buy lists for years. LTIMindtree, formed from the 2022 merger of Larsen & Toubro Infotech and Mindtree, had already carried a reduce rating from Kotak, but the latest report brings its outlook further into negative territory.

Kotak's thesis centers on the accelerating impact of generative AI on traditional IT services revenue. The brokerage has been progressively raising its estimates for AI-driven revenue deflation — from an initial 2–3% assumption earlier this year to approximately 3–3.5% in its March update, factoring in faster adoption by enterprise clients and the automation of software development workflows.

"We expect new opportunities such as legacy modernization to increase, but do not expect them to compensate for the deflation enough."

— Kotak Institutional Equities analysts led by Kawaljeet Saluja

Why Challengers Over Incumbents

The report's preference for mid-tier challengers over established Tier-1 players reflects a growing consensus among analysts that the AI transition will favor nimbler firms with higher revenue growth rates over large incumbents managing massive delivery organizations.

Companies like Coforge, Persistent Systems, and Hexaware have posted stronger revenue growth in recent quarters, with Persistent delivering 16% growth and Coforge expanding by 33%. Their smaller scale allows them to pivot delivery models faster and compete more aggressively for new AI-related implementation and consulting work. Kotak had maintained buy ratings on Coforge and Hexaware in its June coverage.

By contrast, TCS and Infosys face the structural challenge of managing workforces of more than 600,000 and 300,000 employees, respectively, while clients increasingly demand shorter contracts, outcome-based pricing, and AI-augmented delivery that requires fewer billable hours.

Market Impact: Stocks Slide on Multiple Fronts

IT stocks fell sharply following the Kotak downgrade, with TCS and Infosys leading the decline. The sell-off was compounded by renewed concerns over potential changes to the H-1B visa program in the United States, which remains the single most important market for Indian IT services companies.

The Nifty IT index has now declined more than 20% year-to-date, one of the worst-performing sectoral indices on India's exchanges. The sustained decline has erased approximately $73 billion in market value from the sector in 2026 alone, following a 26% drop in 2025. The index's cumulative two-year drawdown has raised fundamental questions about the long-term growth and valuation trajectory of an industry that generates approximately $315 billion in annual revenue.

The sell-off places Indian IT valuations at levels not seen in several years, with Tier-1 companies now trading at approximately 13–18 times FY2028 estimated earnings. Kotak has previously raised its cost-of-equity assumptions for IT companies by 50–100 basis points, reflecting higher structural uncertainty.

A Sector at an Inflection Point

The Kotak report arrives in a year when every major global and domestic brokerage has either downgraded or cut target prices across the Indian IT pack. Jefferies downgraded six Indian IT companies in February, cutting TCS to underperform. CLSA and HSBC followed with their own target price reductions. The mounting consensus is that AI-driven deflation will outpace the new revenue opportunities that AI creates, at least in the medium term.

For India's IT industry — which employs more than five million people and is the largest private-sector employer of skilled workers — the implications extend well beyond stock prices. TCS has already laid off more than 12,000 employees this year, and industry-wide workforce optimization is expected to continue.

Whether the challengers Kotak now favors can sustain their growth premium while navigating the same structural pressures remains an open question. But the brokerage's willingness to walk away from buy ratings on TCS and Infosys — names that have defined Indian IT investing for decades — signals just how fundamentally the AI era is reshaping expectations for the sector.
